title: Milgram (1963) Obedience Study
summary: Comprehensive knowledge base covering Stanley Milgram's 1963 behavioural study of obedience, including aims, sample, methodology, findings, variations, and evaluation points.

knowledge.text: Milgram (1963) conducted a behavioural study titled 'Behavioural study of obedience'.
The aim of Milgram (1963) was to investigate how far people would obey an authority figure instructing them to harm another person.
The sample consisted of 40 American men aged between 20 and 50 years old from New Haven.
Participants were recruited through a newspaper advert via volunteer (self-selected) sampling.
Participants were paid $4.50 for taking part in the study.
The study was conducted in a laboratory setting at Yale University.
The naive participant was always assigned the role of 'teacher'.
A confederate named Mr Wallace was assigned the role of 'learner'.
The teacher gave fake electric shocks to the learner for wrong answers on a word-pair task.
The shock generator ranged from 15V to 450V, increasing in 15V increments.
The experimenter wore a grey lab coat to maintain authority.
Verbal prod 1: 'Please continue'.
Verbal prod 2: 'The experiment requires that you continue'.
Verbal prod 3: 'It is absolutely essential that you continue'.
Verbal prod 4: 'You have no other choice, you must go on'.
The learner pounded on the wall at 300V and became completely silent after 315V.
100% of participants administered shocks up to at least 300V.
65% of participants (26 out of 40) obeyed fully and administered the maximum 450V.
Participants showed signs of extreme tension including sweating, trembling, and nervous laughter.
3 participants experienced full-blown uncontrollable seizures during the procedure.
Milgram concluded that ordinary people will obey orders from a legitimate authority even when it conflicts with their conscience.
The agentic state is a situational explanation where an individual sees themselves as an agent carrying out another person's wishes.
A methodological strength is high control over extraneous variables due to the laboratory setting.
A methodological strength is the use of a standardised procedure, including fixed verbal prods.
In the Bridgeport run-down office variation, obedience to 450V dropped to 47.5%.
In the variation where the experimenter gave orders via telephone, obedience dropped to 20.5%.
An ethical limitation is deception, as participants were misled about the true aim and the reality of the electric shocks.
An ethical limitation is lack of informed consent, because participants were unaware of the true nature of the experiment.
An ethical limitation is psychological harm, evidenced by extreme distress, trembling, and seizures.
An ethical limitation is that verbal prods compromised the participants' right to withdraw.
A sampling limitation is gender bias, as the study used only male participants.
A sampling limitation is cultural bias, as all participants were from the United States.
A limitation is low ecological validity due to the artificial laboratory setting and shock task.
Orne and Holland argued demand characteristics were present because participants may not have believed the shocks were genuine.

intro.text: You are investigating how far ordinary people will obey an authority figure instructing them to harm another person in a laboratory study.
You recruit 40 American men aged 20 to 50 from New Haven using a newspaper advert for $4.50. You assign the naive participant as the teacher.
You test participants using a shock generator ranging from 15V to 450V with 15V increments, while the experimenter wears a grey lab coat.
You watch 65% of participants obey fully to 450V despite extreme distress, leading you to conclude people obey legitimate authority against their conscience.
The agentic state is a situational explanation where an individual sees themselves as an agent carrying out another person's wishes.

sequence.title: Milgram Procedure Steps
sequence.instructions: Jump onto each step in the correct experimental order.

steps.label: Newspaper Recruitment
steps.detail: Participants were recruited through a newspaper advert via volunteer sampling and paid $4.50.

steps.label: Role Assignment
steps.detail: The naive participant was assigned the role of teacher and the confederate Mr Wallace the learner.

steps.label: Word-Pair Task
steps.detail: The teacher gave fake electric shocks ranging from 15V to 450V for wrong answers.

steps.label: Lab Coat Authority
steps.detail: The experimenter wore a grey lab coat and used four mandatory verbal prods.

steps.label: Learner Silence
steps.detail: The learner pounded on the wall at 300V and became completely silent after 315V.

steps.label: Maximum Obedience
steps.detail: 100% shocked to 300V and 65% of participants obeyed fully up to the maximum 450V.

arena.title: Methodological vs Ethical
arena.instructions: Sort each feature into Methodological factors or Ethical factors.

clues.label: Lab Control
clues.claim: High control over extraneous variables due to the laboratory setting.
clues.why: Controlling variables is a methodological strength.

clues.label: Standardisation
clues.claim: Standardised procedure including fixed verbal prods ensured consistency.
clues.why: Standardisation allows replication, representing a strength.

clues.label: Deception
clues.claim: Participants were misled about the true aim and reality of shocks.

clues.label: Distress
clues.claim: Extreme distress, trembling, and seizures caused psychological harm.
clues.why: Causing psychological harm is an ethical limitation.

clues.label: Right to Withdraw
clues.claim: Verbal prods compromised the participants' right to withdraw from the study.
clues.why: Compromising withdrawal rights is an ethical limitation.

clues.label: Sample Bias
clues.claim: Using only American men creates gender and cultural bias.
clues.why: Bias in the sample limits generalisability.

clues.label: Demand Characteristics
clues.claim: Orne and Holland argued participants may not have believed shocks were genuine.
clues.why: Demand characteristics are a methodological limitation.
